summary:
"Abandoned but not Forgotten" is an interactive storytelling website that gives a voice to the equipment humanity left behind on the Moon and Mars. Landers, rovers, instruments and descent stages, from the Apollo 11 Lunar Module to Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter, narrate their own missions in the first person, backed by mission facts and a closing "what happened to me" moment.

Visitors explore Moon and Mars maps with approximate landing sites, a filterable mission timeline, story cards, audio narration, a memorial wall for short tributes, and a quiz. The site retrieves real images from NASA's Image and Video Library, credits NASA on each image, and links to the NSSDC Master Catalog so every story can be verified.

The project addresses the challenge by turning NASA's open data into emotional, memorable storytelling that students and the public can easily understand. It matters because these objects are part of humanity's shared heritage in space. As more countries and companies head to the Moon and Mars, people need to care about preserving landing sites, managing debris and protecting other worlds. The site is free, needs no login, collects no personal data and works on phones and laptops.
details:
What it does: The website presents more than 14 pieces of equipment left on the Moon and Mars as first-person stories. Each story has key facts, a NASA image with credit, an approximate location on an interactive map, and a place on a timeline. Visitors can listen to stories, write a short tribute, and take a quiz.

How it works: It is a static web app. Story data lives in a JSON file and JavaScript renders it into the page. For each artifact, the app requests a public image and metadata from the NASA Image and Video Library API, shows it with NASA credit and a source link, and falls back to an SVG illustration if the network fails. Text-to-speech uses the browser’s Web Speech API. The memorial wall exists only in memory, so no personal data is stored.

Benefits and intended impact: It makes space history engaging for students and the public, encourages respect for historic lunar and Martian sites, and raises awareness of space debris, planetary protection and responsible exploration.

Tools and technologies: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, SVG, Canvas, the NASA Image and Video Library API, the Web Speech API, GitHub, GitHub Pages and Google Slides. AI coding tools helped draft the code and story text, and the team reviewed it.

Creativity: Instead of a standard data dashboard, the machines speak for themselves. Emotional storytelling, the memorial wall and the “then vs now” timeline turn mission data into an experience.

Factors we considered: Accuracy (stories link to NASA sources), accessibility (keyboard navigation, alt text, reduced-motion support, good contrast), no NASA branding, no images of minors, English only, and no personal data collection.
